question: How often does a bounded short-description XOR-mask search beat raw or direct bzip2 on a fixed real-data corpus, and what does the search cost?
compression_ratio_definition: original bytes / complete stored frame bytes; larger is better

framing.transformed: 1-byte family tag || 1-or-2-byte parameters || bzip2(X XOR Y)
framing.tail_policy: Each file tail is a final shorter independent frame.

families.period2: 64 most frequent aligned pairs plus the Cartesian product of the eight most frequent bytes at each parity and four fixed motifs
families.affine8: 64 most frequent (a,b) rules inferred from adjacent bytes plus four fixed rules
families.shake16: 512 fixed seeds from a deterministic permutation of the 65,536-seed family

practical_search.decision_rule: Choose the shortest complete frame; ties use bytewise frame order, which prefers raw/direct tags over transformed tags.

exact_validation.selection_rule: Select complete chunks with the lexicographically smallest SHA-256 digests before examining compression results.

chunks.selection_rule: smallest SHA-256 among complete 4096-byte chunks; independent of compression result

limitations: The fixed Canterbury Corpus is a benchmark corpus, not a probabilistic model of all user workloads.
Chunks are compressed independently, so results do not equal whole-file bzip2 sizes.
The bounded search reports performance for its declared candidate budget, not all possible generation rules.
Exact-search recall is measured on six predeclared hash-selected chunks and is not a proof for every chunk.
Search wall time is platform-specific and is not included in stored bytes.
The 16-bit SHAKE seed is a compression codebook index and offers no encryption security.
